# Day 1: Introduction to R & RStudio

## Today's Plan

- Why R for clinical research
- R vs RStudio: install and the interface
- Projects, scripts, objects and vectors
- Data frames and packages (tidyverse)
- Importing and a first look at the study data
- Hands-on exercise

::: {.notes}
Key point: this whole day is about getting comfortable, not memorising. By tonight every participant will have imported a real clinical dataset and looked at it.

Common misconception: that you must be a programmer. You do not; R is a tool like a calculator or a stethoscope.

Clinical interpretation: reproducible analysis means a colleague or a regulator can re-run your work and get the same numbers.

Ask the audience: who has used Excel for research? Expected answer: almost everyone. Bridge: R does what Excel does, but it records every step.

Demo tip: keep RStudio open on screen behind you so people see the real thing, not just slides.
:::

## Why R for Clinical Research {.smaller}

### What R gives you

| A free, open-source language for statistics and data
| Used in clinical trials, epidemiology and journals
| Handles import, cleaning, analysis and plots in one place

### Why it matters

| Every step is written down, so the analysis is repeatable
| No cost and no licence: install on any computer
| A huge community and packages for medical research

::: {.callout-note}
## Reproducibility
If you can re-run the script, you can defend the result.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: the headline advantage is reproducibility plus zero cost. Click-by-click in Excel is hard to reproduce; a script is the recipe.

Common misconception: that free means low quality. R is used by FDA, EMA reviewers, and most major epidemiology groups.

Clinical interpretation: when a reviewer asks how you derived a number, you point to a line of code, not your memory.

Ask the audience: what happens if you redo last year's analysis in Excel by hand? Expected answer: you may get slightly different numbers. A script removes that risk.

Demo tip: mention that the figures in many NEJM and Lancet papers are made in R.
:::

## R vs RStudio: Two Different Things

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### R (the engine)

- The actual statistical language
- Does the computation
- You install it first
- Rarely opened on its own
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### RStudio (the dashboard)

- A friendly workspace around R
- Editor, console, plots, help
- Install it second
- This is what you open daily
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Key point: R is the engine, RStudio is the dashboard. You need both, and you install R first.

Common mistake: people try to open R directly and find a bare console. Always open RStudio instead.

Clinical interpretation: think of R as the lab analyser and RStudio as the technician's interface to it.

Ask the audience: which one do you double-click each morning? Expected answer: RStudio.

Demo tip: show both icons on the desktop so the distinction is concrete.
:::

## The RStudio Interface: Four Panes {.smaller}

### Top-left: Source (Script editor)

| Where you write and save your code

### Bottom-left: Console

| Where code runs and results appear

### Top-right: Environment

| The objects and data you have created

### Bottom-right: Files / Plots / Help

| Folders, your graphs, and documentation

::: {.callout-tip}
## Orientation
Spend two minutes finding each pane before you type.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: just four panes. Source and Console on the left, Environment and the Files/Plots/Help tabs on the right.

Common misconception: that the layout is fixed; it is configurable, but the defaults are fine for beginners.

Clinical interpretation: the Environment pane is your worktop, it shows what data is currently loaded.

Ask the audience: where will a graph appear? Expected answer: bottom-right, the Plots tab.

Demo tip: type a line in the Console and the same line in the Source, and show that only the saved Source persists.
:::

## RStudio Projects and the Working Directory

### The working directory

| The folder R looks in when you open a file
| Check it with getwd()

### Use a Project, not setwd()

| File \> New Project keeps everything in one folder
| Paths become relative, like Data/file.csv
| The work runs on any computer, unchanged

::: {.callout-warning}
## Avoid setwd()
A hard-coded path breaks on every other machine.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: an RStudio Project sets the working directory for you and makes paths portable.

Common mistake: setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/...") at the top of a script. It works only on that one computer.

Clinical interpretation: portability matters when you share an analysis with a statistician or a collaborator at another site.

Ask the audience: what is wrong with writing the full C: path? Expected answer: nobody else has that exact folder.

Demo tip: run getwd() once so people see what the current folder actually is, then open the course Project.
:::

## Script vs Console

[Both run R code, but only one is your record.]{.slide-intro}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Console

- Type, press Enter, get an answer
- Good for quick tries
- Not saved when you close
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Script (Source)

- You write, then save as a .R file
- Re-run any time, line by line
- This is your reproducible record
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Key point: the script is the reproducible record; the console is a scratchpad.

Common misconception: that typing in the console is enough. It vanishes on close.

Clinical interpretation: the saved script is your analysis audit trail, like a signed lab notebook.

Ask the audience: where should the real analysis live? Expected answer: in a saved script.

Demo tip: run a line with Ctrl+Enter from the script and show the result appearing in the console below.
:::

## First Steps: R as a Calculator

[The simplest way to start - just type sums into the Console.]{.slide-intro}

```r
2 + 2
140 / 90        # a blood-pressure ratio
sqrt(16)
(120 + 130 + 145 + 150) / 4   # mean of four readings
```

```{.text .code-output}
[1] 4
[1] 1.555556
[1] 4
[1] 136.25
```

::: {.code-note}
Everything in R is built from small steps like these - start simple, then build up.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: R is first and foremost a calculator - functions like sqrt() and arithmetic (+, -, \*, /) work exactly as you expect.

Common misconception: that you must memorise commands before you can do anything. You can explore by just typing sums.

Clinical interpretation: a blood-pressure ratio or a quick mean of a few readings is real, useful work on day one.

Audience question: what does 140 / 90 give, and what might it represent? Expected answer: about 1.56 - a crude systolic-to-diastolic ratio.

Demo tip: let participants call out sums and type them live; build confidence before introducing objects.
:::

## Objects and the Assignment Arrow

### Store a value in an object

| sbp \<- 152 means store 152 in an object named sbp
| Type the name sbp to print it back
| The arrow \<- is the assignment operator

### R is case-sensitive

| SBP and sbp are two different objects

::: {.callout-important}
## Common slips
Using = instead of \<-; mixing up upper and lower case.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: \<- stores a value in a named object; the name then behaves like the value.

Common mistake: writing sbp = 152 (works but is discouraged) or calling it Sbp later and getting an error.

Clinical interpretation: an object is just a labelled container, like a labelled specimen tube.

Ask the audience: is Age the same as age in R? Expected answer: no, R is case-sensitive.

Demo tip: type the shortcut Alt+- (Alt and minus) to insert \<- automatically, and show the case-sensitivity error live.
:::

## Objects and Vectors in Action

[A vector holds many values of the same type.]{.slide-intro}

```r
sbp <- 152
sbp
sbp_readings <- c(152, 138, 145, 160, 129, 142)
length(sbp_readings)
mean(sbp_readings)
sd(sbp_readings)
```

```{.text .code-output}
[1] 152
[1] 6
[1] 144.3333
[1] 11.23239
```

::: {.code-note}
c() means combine; mean() and sd() summarise the whole vector.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: c() combines values into a vector; functions like length(), mean() and sd() act on the whole vector at once.

Common mistake: forgetting the commas inside c(), or mixing text and numbers in one vector.

Clinical interpretation: a vector is one column of readings, six systolic measurements here.

Ask the audience: what does length() tell us? Expected answer: how many values are in the vector, here six.

Demo tip: also run summary(sbp\_readings) and max(sbp\_readings) so they see more functions on the same object.
:::

## Data Types You Will Meet

### Three everyday types

| numeric: numbers, like age or sbp (60, 152)
| character: text in quotes, like "Female"
| logical: TRUE or FALSE, like sbp \>= 140

### Why type matters

| You can average numbers, not text
| R picks the type when it reads your data

::: {.callout-note}
## Tip
glimpse() shows the type of every column at a glance.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: numeric, character and logical are the three types beginners need. Each column of data is one type.

Common misconception: that a number stored as text behaves like a number; it does not, you cannot average it.

Clinical interpretation: if age was imported as text (because of a stray value like 200 or a letter), means will fail until it is fixed.

Ask the audience: what type is "Yes"/"No"? Expected answer: character text; we will recode it later.

Demo tip: create high\_bp \<- sbp\_readings \>= 140 and show the TRUE/FALSE logical vector, then sum() it to count.
:::

## Data Frames and Tibbles

### The shape of a dataset

| A data frame is a table: rows and columns
| Each row is one patient (one observation)
| Each column is one variable (age, sex, sbp)

### Tibble

| The tidyverse version of a data frame
| Prints neatly and shows column types

::: {.callout-note}
## Read it as a clinic
Rows are people; columns are what you measured.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: a data frame (or tibble) is the rectangular table that holds your study, rows = patients, columns = variables.

Common misconception: that R data looks like a spreadsheet with merged cells and colours; it is plain tidy columns.

Clinical interpretation: this rows-are-patients, columns-are-variables layout is exactly the tidy structure analyses expect.

Ask the audience: in our data, what does one row represent? Expected answer: one adult attending a PHC facility.

Demo tip: contrast a tibble print (clean, shows types) with a base data.frame print so they appreciate tibbles.
:::

## Packages: Install Once, Load Each Session

### Two different commands

| install.packages("tidyverse") downloads it once
| library(tidyverse) loads it every new session

### Packages we use today

| tidyverse: import, wrangle, plot
| readxl: read Excel .xlsx files

::: {.callout-important}
## Common mistake
Running install.packages() every time (slow, needs internet).
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: install once (downloads from the internet), library() every time you start R. Two separate jobs.

Common mistake: putting install.packages() at the top of a script that runs daily; it re-downloads needlessly and fails offline.

Clinical interpretation: a package is a toolbox of extra functions; tidyverse and readxl are the ones we need for import.

Ask the audience: do you install a package every session? Expected answer: no, you only library() it.

Demo tip: show library(tidyverse) printing its attaching message, and note that is normal, not an error.
:::

## Importing the Study Data

[Load packages first, then read the file.]{.slide-intro}

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
htn <- read_csv("Data/hypertension_phc_raw.csv")
htn_xl <- read_excel(
  "Data/hypertension_phc_raw.xlsx", sheet = "data")
dim(htn)
```

```{.text .code-output}
Rows: 1503  Columns: 36
[1] 1503   36
```

::: {.code-note}
read\_csv for CSV, read\_excel for Excel. Note 1503, not 1500.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: read\_csv() reads the CSV, read\_excel() reads the Excel; both land in a tibble. The paths are relative because we are in a Project.

Common mistake: forgetting library(readxl) before read\_excel, or a wrong path/file name (case and spelling must match exactly).

Clinical interpretation: 1503 rows but the study enrolled 1,500, so three duplicate records are hiding in here.

Ask the audience: why 1503 and not 1500? Expected answer: there are 3 duplicate records, which we fix on Day 2.

Demo tip: point out the column specification message read\_csv prints; it is informational, not an error.
:::

## First Look: Knowing Your Data {.smaller}

[Run these the moment any dataset is imported.]{.slide-intro}

- dim(htn): how many rows and columns
- names(htn): the variable names
- glimpse(htn): every column with its type
- head(htn): the first few rows
- View(htn): open the spreadsheet viewer
- htn\$age: pull one column out with the dollar sign
- summary(htn\$age): min, mean, max of a variable
- table(htn\$sex): counts of each category

::: {.notes}
Key point: a fixed first-look routine, dim, names, glimpse, head, View, then \$ to inspect single variables with summary and table.

Common mistake: jumping straight to analysis without looking; many data problems are visible in the first thirty seconds.

Clinical interpretation: summary() and table() are your screening tests for the data; they flag impossible values and messy categories.

Ask the audience: what does htn\$age return? Expected answer: the age column as a single vector.

Demo tip: run View(htn) so people see the familiar spreadsheet grid, then close it and rely on glimpse().
:::

## Inspecting Single Variables

[The \$ extracts one column to summarise.]{.slide-intro}

```r
summary(htn$age)
table(htn$sex)
```

```{.text .code-output}
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
   0.0    38.0    52.0    53.4    66.0   200.0

     f      F female Female      m ...
    11     63    402    498     14 ...
```

::: {.code-note}
Max age 200 and eight spellings of sex: this data needs cleaning.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: summary() on age and table() on sex immediately expose problems, an impossible max of 200 and many spellings of the same category.

Common misconception: that imported data is clean; raw clinical data almost never is.

Clinical interpretation: an age of 200 (and a 0) cannot be real; Female/female/F/f are all the same group recorded inconsistently.

Ask the audience: how many true sex categories should there be? Expected answer: two, but the table shows eight labels.

Demo tip: also run table(htn\$facility) to reveal stray spaces, and tell them Day 2 fixes all of this.
:::

## Common Mistakes and Quick Debugging

### When it does not work, check

| Did you run library() for the package?
| Did you use \<- and not = for assignment?
| Is the spelling and CASE exactly right?
| Is the file path and name correct?

::: {.callout-warning}
## could not find function
Usually means the package is not loaded: run library().
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## cannot open file
Wrong path or file name; check the Files pane.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: most beginner errors are one of four things, missing library(), wrong operator, a case/spelling slip, or a bad path.

Common mistake: panicking at red text. Read the message; it usually names the problem.

Clinical interpretation: debugging is like differential diagnosis, read the sign (the error), form a hypothesis, test the fix.

Ask the audience: you get could not find function read\_csv, what is wrong? Expected answer: tidyverse is not loaded; run library(tidyverse).

Demo tip: deliberately trigger one error live (mistype the file name) and walk through reading the message calmly.
:::

## What the Data Is Already Telling Us

### Problems visible on the first look

| Age = 200 and age = 0: impossible values
| Sex recorded eight different ways
| 1503 rows for 1,500 people: duplicates

### Why this is good news

| We found it in seconds, before any analysis
| Cleaning is the topic of Day 2

::: {.callout-note}
## Garbage in, garbage out
No statistic is trustworthy on uncleaned data.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: the first look has already surfaced the three big issues, impossible values, inconsistent categories, and duplicate rows.

Common misconception: that finding problems means you did something wrong; finding them early is exactly the goal.

Clinical interpretation: analysing before cleaning would bias every result, the mean age would be pulled up by the 200.

Ask the audience: should we calculate mean age right now? Expected answer: no, fix the impossible values first.

Demo tip: foreshadow Day 2 by showing how a single 200 distorts mean(htn\$age); it motivates the cleaning day.
:::

## Day 1 Exercise: Import the Clinical Dataset

### Your tasks

| Open the course RStudio Project
| library(tidyverse) and library(readxl)
| Import the CSV with read\_csv()
| Import the Excel file with read\_excel()
| Run glimpse() on the data
| summary() the age column, table() the sex column

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to notice
Spot the impossible age, the many sex spellings, 1503 rows.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: the exercise is the whole Day 1 workflow end to end, project, packages, import both formats, then inspect.

Common mistake: forgetting a library() call, or a path typo; circulate and check these first.

Clinical interpretation: by importing and inspecting, participants experience the same data-quality red flags we just discussed.

Ask the audience: after table(sex), how many distinct labels do you see? Expected answer: eight, for two real categories.

Demo tip: give a fixed time (about 15 minutes), then debrief by asking who found the age of 200 first.
:::

### Today you learned to

| Tell R from RStudio and find the four panes
| Work in a Project with a saved script
| Make objects (\<-) and vectors (c())
| Load packages and import CSV and Excel data
| Inspect data with glimpse, summary and table

### Tomorrow: Day 2

| Cleaning the mess: fix ages, unify categories
| Remove duplicates and handle missing values

::: {.callout-note}
## Well done
You imported real clinical data on day one.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: consolidate the arc, from never having opened R to importing and inspecting a real dataset, then preview cleaning.

Common misconception: that we will start analysing tomorrow; first we clean, because trustworthy analysis needs clean data.

Clinical interpretation: today was data IN and a first look; Day 2 turns the raw, messy file into an analysis-ready dataset.

Ask the audience: what are the three data problems we must fix tomorrow? Expected answer: impossible values, inconsistent categories, duplicate rows.

Demo tip: end by re-opening their script and re-running it top to bottom, proving reproducibility in one keystroke.
:::
